{{Short description|Extinct Austronesian language of Taiwan}} {{Infobox language | name = Siraya | altname = Siraiya | states = [[Taiwan]] | region = Southwestern, around present-day [[Tainan]] | extinct = end of 19th century; revitalization movement |revived= 2020s | familycolor = Austronesian | fam2 = [[East Formosan languages|East Formosan]] | fam3 = [[Sirayaic languages|Sirayaic]] | script = {{ubl|[[Latin script|Latin]] (modern Siraya alphabet)|[[Latin script|Latin]] ([[Sinkang Manuscripts]])}} | iso3 = fos | map = Formosan languages 2008.png | mapcaption = (pink) Siraya | coordinates = {{coord|22|58|N|120|18|E|type:landmark|display=inline}} | glotto = sira1267 | glottoname = Sirayaic | glotto2 = nucl1578 | glottoname2 = Siraya | lingua = 30-FAA-b }} '''Siraya''' is a [[Formosan languages|Formosan language]] spoken until the end of the 19th century by the indigenous [[Siraya people]] of [[Taiwan]], derived from [[Proto-Siraya language|Proto-Siraya]]. Some scholars believe [[Taivoan language|Taivoan]] and [[Makatao language|Makatao]] are two dialects of Siraya, but now more evidence shows that they should be classified as separate languages. Several Siraya communities have been involved in a Sirayan cultural and [[language revitalization]] movement for more than a decade. Through linguistic research and language teaching, the natives are 'awaking' their ancestors mother tongue that has been 'dormant' for a century. Today a group of Siraya children in [[Sinhua District, Tainan|Sinhua District]] of [[Tainan]] particularly in Kou-pei and Chiou Chen Lin area are able to speak and sing in the Siraya language.[http://www.tatalag.org.tw Musu hapa Siraya] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080906193501/http://www.tatalag.org.tw/ |date=2008-09-06 }} {{in lang|zh}} ==Dialects== {{See also|Taivoan language}} The Sirayaic languages were previously thought to include three languages or dialects: *Siraya proper — spoken in the coastal area of Tainan Plain. *Taivoan — spoken mostly in the inland of Tainan Plain to the north (just west of Southern Tsouic territories). *Makatao — spoken in Kaohsiung and Pingtung Prefectures to the south (just west of Paiwan territories). However, more and more evidences have shown that Siraya, Taivoan, and Makatao are three different languages, rather than three dialects: === Documentary evidence === In "De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia" written by the Dutch colonizers during 1629–1662, it was clearly said that when the Dutch people would like to speak to the chieftain of Cannacannavo ([[Kanakanavu people|Kanakanavu]]), they needed to translate from [[Dutch language|Dutch]] to Sinckan (Siraya), from Sinckan to [[Tarroequan]] (possibly a [[Paiwan language|Paiwan]] or a [[Rukai language|Rukai]] language), from Tarroequan to [[Taivoan language|Taivoan]], and from Taivoan to [[Kanakanavu language|Cannacannavo]].{{Cite book |url=http://resources.huygens.knaw.nl/retroboeken/taiwan/ |title=De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia, Taiwan: 1629–1662 |date=1986 |publisher=M. Nijhoff |location=ʼS-Gravenhage}}{{Cite book|title=From Single to Group: The Formation of Sideia in the 17th Century|last=Lee|first=Jui-Yuan|publisher=Department of History: National Cheng Kung University|year=2015}}
"...... in Cannacannavo: Aloelavaos tot welcken de vertolckinge in Sinccans, Tarrocquans en Tevorangs geschiede, weder voor een jaer aengenomen" — "De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia", pp.6–8

Lee (2015) regards that, when Siraya was a [[lingua franca]] among at least eight indigenous communities in southwestern Taiwan plain, [[Taivoan people]] from Tevorangh, who has been proved to have their own language in "De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia", might still need the translation service from Wanli, a neighbor community that shared common hunting field and also a militarily alliance with Tevorangh. ==Sources== [[Image:Gospel of St. Matthew in Formosan.jpg|left|thumb|200px|Gospel of St. Matthew in Dutch, Sinckan, and English.{{sfnp|Campbell|Gravius|1888|p=1}} Original Dutch and Sinckan above is from 1661 by [[Daniel Gravius]]; English in small type was added in 1888 by Scottish missionary [[William Campbell (missionary)|William Campbell]].]] The Siraya language entered the historical record in the early 17th century when traders from the [[Dutch East India Company]], expelled from [[mainland China]] and Chinese waters, set up a stronghold on Taiwan at [[Fort Zeelandia (Taiwan)|Fort Zeelandia]], which was in the Siraya-speaking area. During the period of [[Dutch Formosa|Dutch rule in Taiwan]], [[Calvinism|Calvinist]] missionaries used Siraya and [[Babuza language|Babuza]] (also known as ''Favorlang'') as contact languages. A translation of the Gospel of St. Matthew into Siraya (174 pages of Siraya and Dutch text, Gravius 1661){{cite book |last=Gravius |first=Daniel |author-link=Daniel Gravius |year=1661 |title=Het heylige Euangelium Matthei en Johannis. Ofte Hagnau ka d'llig matiktik ka na sasoulat ti Mattheus ti Johannes appa |place=Amsterdam |publisher=Michiel Hartogh |oclc=69326189 }}{{cite book |title=The Gospel of St. Matthew in Formosan (Sinkang dialect) with corresponding versions in Dutch and English |last1=Campbell |first1=William |author1-link=William Campbell (missionary) |last2=Gravius |first2=Daniel |publisher= Trubner |place=London |year=1888 |language=fos, nl, en |oclc=844610148}} and a catechism in Siraya (288 pages of Siraya and Dutch text, Gravius 1662){{cite book |last=Gravius |first=Daniel |year=1661 |title=Patar ki tna-'msing-an ki Christang ofte. 't Formulier des Christendoms. |place=Amsterdam |publisher=Michiel Hartogh |oclc=846467128 }} were published, and have been subsequently republished.{{cite journal |last=Adelaar |first=K. A. |year=1997 |title=Grammar Notes on Siraya, An Extinct Formosan Language |journal=Oceanic Linguistics |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=362–397 |jstor=3622990 |doi=10.2307/3622990 |language=en }} The Dutch colony was driven out in 1661 by [[Ming Dynasty|Ming]] loyalist refugees from China, and Taiwan was subsequently incorporated into the [[Qing Dynasty|Qing]] Empire. During the period of [[Taiwan under Qing Dynasty rule|Qing Dynasty rule]], use of Siraya receded, but some Siraya language materials survive in the form of Siraya land contracts with Chinese translations, known as the [[Sinckan Manuscripts]]. The last records were lists of words made in the early 19th century. The Tainan Pe-po Siraya Culture Association published a modern-day Siraya glossary in 2008, authored by Edgar Macapili.i.e., {{Cite book |last=Macapili |first=Edgar 萬益嘉 |date=2008 |publisher=Tainan Pe-po Siraya Culture Association |location=Tainan |script-title=zh:Siraya Glossary: Based on the Gospel of St. Matthew in Formosan (Sinkan Dialect): A Preliminary Survey / 西拉雅詞彙初探: 以新港語馬太福音硏究為主例}} A paper published in 2021 reports on a translation of the Gospel of St. John that had recently been identified by the author in the [[Royal Danish Library]].{{Cite journal |last=Joby |first=Christopher |date=2020 |title=A Recently Discovered Copy of a Translation of the Gospel of St. John in Siraya |journal=Oceanic Linguistics |language=en |volume=59 |issue=1–2 |pages=212–231 |doi=10.1353/ol.2020.0011|s2cid=234958672 }} ==Phonology== The phonological system of Siraya is speculated by Adelaar (1997) to have the following [[phoneme]]s. '''Demonstratives''' *atta, k(a)-atta 'this, these' *anna, k(a)-anna 'that, those' '''Interrogatives''' *mang 'what?' *ti mang 'who?' *tu mang 'where' *mama mang, mama ki mang, mameymang 'how?' *kaumang 'why?' '''Negation markers''' *assi (also "aoussi") 'no(t)' *ĭnna{{hamza}} don't' *nĭnno 'nothing' *mi-kakua.. . assi ("myhkaqua ... assi") 'never' *ĭnnang ("ynnang") 'refuse to, not want to; don't' '''Other words''' *''ti'' – personal article *''ta'' – topic marker *''tu'' – locative marker *''ki'' – default relation marker *''tu ämäx ki'' – "before" *''tu lam ki'' – "together with" *''ka'' – coordinating conjunction (links verbal clauses) ===Verbs=== The following list of Siraya verb affixes is from Adelaar (1997). ;Affixes *ni-: past tense *ma-, m-, -m-: actor focus / orientation *pa-: undergoer focus / orientation *mey- ~ pey-: actor- and undergoer-oriented verbs (used with verbs describing a high degree of physical involvement) *mu- ~ (p)u-: actor- and undergoer-oriented verbs (used with verbs describing a movement toward something) *ma-: stative intransitive verbs; words with no apparent word-class affiliations (precategorials) *paka-: causative *pa-: transitive (often with causative result) *ka-: expresses feeling, emotion, sensation (undergoer-oriented verbs and deverbal nouns only) *-ən, -an: undergoer focus / orientation *-a, -ey, -aw: irrealis *-(l)ato: possibly a perfective marker See also ''[[Proto-Austronesian language]]'' for a list of Proto-Austronesian verbal affixes. ;Classifiers Like [[Bunun language|Bunun]] and many other [[Formosan languages]], Siraya has a rich set of verbal classifier prefixes. *mattäy- / pattäy-: "talking, saying" *smaki-: "throwing, casting" *sau-: "swearing, making an oath" *mu-, pu-: movement into a certain direction *mey- / pey-: high degree of physical involvement *sa-: movement through a narrow place *taw-: downward movement, a movement within a confined space ==Numerals== Siraya has a base ten [[numeral system]] with the following forms: {| class="wikitable" |+Siraya Numerals !
